title: How does a composite (multi-column) index work and what is the left-prefix rule (an index on `(a, b)` serves `WHERE a` and `WHERE a AND b` but NOT `WHERE b` alone), and why put equality columns before range columns?
shortTitle: How does a composite index work and what is the left-prefix rule — why put equality columns before range columns

s1_definition.profdef: A composite index is a single B-tree built over an ordered list of columns, sorting rows first by the first column, then by the second within equal values of the first, and so on. The left-prefix rule states that the index can efficiently serve any query that filters a contiguous prefix of its columns starting from the leftmost: an index on `(a, b)` serves `WHERE a` and `WHERE a AND b`, but not `WHERE b` alone, because without a value for `a` there is no single contiguous range to seek. Equality columns should precede range columns because once a range predicate is applied to a column, the ordering of all columns after it is no longer usable for further seeking.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India phone directory, sorted first by branch, then by customer surname within each branch. That is a composite index on (branch, surname). You can instantly find "everyone in the Mumbai branch" (uses the first column) or "the Sharmas in Mumbai" (uses both). But you cannot use this directory to find "all Sharmas everywhere" quickly, because the Sharmas are scattered across every branch section — there is no single block to flip to. That is the left-prefix rule. And if you first ask for "branches between A and M," the surnames inside that wide range are no longer in one tidy block, which is why you want the exact-match column first and the range column last.
s1_definition.oneliner: A composite index is sorted left to right, so it serves a leftmost prefix of its columns — put equality columns first and the single range column last.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A composite index is a single B-tree built over an ordered list of columns, sorting rows first by the first column, then by the second within equal values of the first, and so on. The left-prefix rule states that the index can efficiently serve any query that filters a contiguous prefix of its columns starting from the leftmost: an index on `(a, b)` serves `WHERE a` and `WHERE a AND b`, but not `WHERE b` alone, because without a value for `a` there is no single contiguous range to seek. Equality columns should precede range columns because once a range predicate is applied to a column, the ordering of all columns after it is no longer usable for further seeking.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India phone directory, sorted first by branch, then by customer surname within each branch. That is a composite index on (branch, surname). You can instantly find "everyone in the Mumbai branch" (uses the first column) or "the Sharmas in Mumbai" (uses both). But you cannot use this directory to find "all Sharmas everywhere" quickly, because the Sharmas are scattered across every branch section — there is no single block to flip to. That is the left-prefix rule. And if you first ask for "branches between A and M," the surnames inside that wide range are no longer in one tidy block, which is why you want the exact-match column first and the range column last.

**One line to remember:** A composite index is sorted left to right, so it serves a leftmost prefix of its columns — put equality columns first and the single range column last.

sections.s2_technical:
A composite index on `(account_id, created_at)` physically sorts its entries first by `account_id`, and then, within each account, by `created_at`. This is why it perfectly serves `WHERE account_id = ? ORDER BY created_at`: it seeks to the account and the dates are already in order beneath it.

The left-prefix rule falls directly out of that sort order. The index can seek efficiently only when it can identify a single contiguous range of entries. `WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001'` identifies one contiguous block, so it is served. `WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'` narrows within that block, also served. But `WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'` alone cannot be served efficiently, because entries for that date range are scattered across every account; there is no single block to seek, so the engine would have to scan the whole index or the table.

The ordering of equality before range columns matters because of how B-tree seeking works. An equality predicate pins a column to a single value, keeping the remaining columns perfectly ordered beneath it. A range predicate opens the column to many values, after which the next column's values are interleaved across that range and no longer form a single sorted run usable for seeking. So for `WHERE account_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, the right index is `(account_id, created_at)` — equality first, range last — which seeks to the account and then walks the date range. Reversing it to `(created_at, account_id)` would force scanning the whole date range and filtering accounts within it.

A senior nuance: a composite index can also be a skip-scan candidate in some engines when the leading column has very few distinct values, but you should never rely on that; design the column order for your real predicates. Another nuance is that column order also affects ORDER BY — the index can avoid a sort only if the query's sort columns are a prefix of the index in the same direction. And a composite index on `(a, b)` still helps `WHERE a` alone, so you often do not need a separate single-column index on `a`.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The statement screen runs `WHERE account_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`. This is the textbook case for a composite index with the equality column first and the range column last.

Problem 2 — A developer added a separate index on `created_at` alone hoping to speed a "transactions across all accounts in a date range" report, but the composite `(account_id, created_at)` could not serve `WHERE created_at` alone because of the left-prefix rule. This shows why the leading column matters.

Problem 3 — Someone proposed `(created_at, account_id)` for the statement query. This is exactly the wrong order: the range on the leading column destroys seekability for the account filter.

The mini-project builds a statement service with the correct composite index, demonstrates that a query on the second column alone does not use it, and shows why equality-before-range wins by comparing both column orders in the plan.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/composite-index-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# USES the composite index (equality first, range last)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE account_id='SAV2001' AND created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-01';"

# Left prefix: account_id alone still uses the index
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001';"

# Second column alone → left-prefix rule → Seq Scan (index not usable)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-01';"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a statement request for SAV2001 between January and March, then a date-only report across all accounts.

Step 1 — The statement query has an equality predicate on account id and a range on created-at. The composite index is sorted first by account id, so the engine seeks straight to the SAV2001 block.

Step 2 — Within the SAV2001 block, entries are already sorted by created-at, so the engine walks from the lower date bound to the upper bound, reading TXN001 and TXN002 in order and stopping at the boundary.

Step 3 — The engine never examines CUR3001's entries at all, because they are in a different part of the index. This is the equality-first payoff: the account filter pins a single contiguous block, and the range walks cleanly within it.

Step 4 — The date-only report filters just created-at. Because created-at is the second column, its values are scattered across every account's block; there is no single contiguous range to seek, so the left-prefix rule means the index cannot be used and the planner falls back to a scan.

Step 5 — The plans confirm the behavior: Index Scan for the account-plus-date query and the account-only query, but Sequential Scan for the date-only query, exactly as the left-prefix rule predicts.

```text
2026-10-25 15:09:09 INFO    StatementService - Composite seek: account SAV2001 (equality) + date range (uses ix_acct_date)
2026-10-25 15:09:09 WARNING StatementService - Date-only filter cannot use ix_acct_date (left-prefix rule) → scan
```


sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Composite Index & Left-Prefix ═══

  ┌─ Rules ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Index (a, b) sorts by a then b within each a             │
  │  Serves WHERE a  and  WHERE a AND b                       │
  │  Does NOT serve WHERE b alone (left-prefix rule)          │
  │  Equality columns FIRST, the single range column LAST     │
  │  Range on a column kills seekability of columns after it  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          StatementService           │
  │  + statement(id, from, to): List    │ equality+range → index
  │  + allAccountsByDate(from,to): List │ second col only → scan
  └───────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                  │ «interface»
                  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        TransactionRepository        │
  │  findByAccountIdAndCreatedAtBetween │ ✓ ix_acct_date
  │  findByAccountId                    │ ✓ left prefix
  │  findByCreatedAtBetween             │ ✗ scan
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Service.statement("SAV2001", Jan, Mar)
  2.   → Repo.findByAccountIdAndCreatedAtBetween(...)
  3.     → seek SAV2001 (equality) → walk date range
  4.   → 2 rows, no sort, CUR3001 untouched
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A composite index is a single B-tree built over an ordered list of columns, and the key insight is that it sorts rows first by the leftmost column, then by the next column within equal values of the first, and so on. Because of that sort order it obeys the left-prefix rule: an index on columns a and b can efficiently serve a query that filters a leftmost prefix — a WHERE on a, or a WHERE on a and b together — but it cannot efficiently serve a WHERE on b alone, because the b values are scattered across every a value and there is no single contiguous block to seek.

The reason you put equality columns before range columns follows from how B-tree seeking works. An equality predicate pins a column to one value and keeps every column after it perfectly ordered, so the next column can still be seeked. A range predicate opens a column to many values, and after that the following columns are interleaved across the range and no longer form a single sorted run. So for a query that filters an account exactly and a date by range, the right index order is account first and date second: seek to the account, then walk the date range within it.

At the National Bank of India our statement query filtered by account id with equality and by created-at with a range. I built the composite index as account id then created-at, and the plan showed a clean index seek that touched only that customer's rows and needed no sort. When a teammate proposed reversing the order to created-at then account id, I showed with EXPLAIN that it degraded into scanning the whole date range and filtering accounts inside it, which was far slower.

The nuance I always raise is that this same index also serves a query on account id alone, because that is a valid left prefix, so we did not need a separate single-column index on account id. But a report that filtered only by date could not use it at all, and that was the clearest demonstration of the left-prefix rule in practice — I verified every one of these conclusions with the execution plan rather than assuming.
